unit: per job: one front heater core, replaced. All four examples are the big kind of job, where the heater/air-conditioning box behind the dashboard has to be opened or removed (dashboard out or partly out, and on most of these the A/C system opened). Hours include draining and refilling coolant; the manufacturer times used also include a diagnosis step and a cooling-system flush. Not included: A/C refrigerant recovery and recharge where billed separately, new coolant, hoses, and any rear heater core. Vehicles whose heater core slides out without removing the dashboard are a much smaller job and are not represented by these examples

finding: The live range of $240-$1,850 is far too low at the bottom and about right to slightly low at the top. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2016 Mazda3 about $695-$1,975 (4.7-10 hr); midsize 2016 Mazda CX-5 about $707-$2,294 (4.8-10 hr); truck 2016 F-150 about $991-$1,693 (7.7-9.4 hr); luxury 2015 Infiniti Q70 about $1,347-$2,164 (7.8-10 hr). All four examples are the big kind of job (heater box behind the dashboard opened or removed), which is what most modern vehicles need. The lowest total we can build is about $695, and that uses an aftermarket core at an online price plus a manufacturer warranty time; the lowest benchmark figure is $500 (AutoZone), and RepairPal's national average starts at $1,375. Nothing found supports $240 for a dashboard-out vehicle. Some vehicles do have a heater core that comes out without removing the dashboard, and those cost far less: a Volkswagen bulletin for the 2013-2014 Passat TDI lists heater core remove-and-reinstall at 160 time units plus 30 for the replacement, against 100 for a coolant drain and fill, but we did not load a source for converting Volkswagen time units to hours, so no figure for the small kind of job is given and no parts price was collected for it. A floor of roughly $500-$700 fits what was found for the common, big kind. The $1,850 top is in line with RepairPal ($1,912) and is exceeded by our highest totals, which combine a genuine core at list price with 10 hours. How solid the labor times are: all four low ends are manufacturer warranty times for the example vehicle itself (Mazda 4.7 and 4.8 hr, Ford 7.7-9.4 hr, Infiniti 7.8 hr), and each includes a diagnosis or flush step, so they slightly overstate the bare swap but are still the low end of what a shop bills. The Ford range is entirely Ford's own figures across cab layouts and engines. The 10-hour high end for the Mazda and Infiniti examples is the top of a parts retailer's general 'four to ten hours' statement, not a figure for those vehicles, and is probably generous for the Mazdas. The Mazda, Ford and Infiniti bulletins do not say in words that the dashboard is removed or the A/C evacuated; that is inferred from their parts lists and times. For the Infiniti no aftermarket core was found, so its low parts figure is a discounted genuine part.
extras: A quote often adds diagnosis (pressure test, confirming the leak or blockage), new coolant and a cooling-system flush, A/C refrigerant recovery and recharge when the A/C has to be opened (a GM bulletin lists 0.3 hr extra for R-134a systems and 1.2 hr for R-1234yf, plus the refrigerant), heater hoses, clamps and O-rings, shop supplies and sales tax. Shops often suggest replacing the A/C evaporator or blend-door actuators while the dashboard is out. A clogged core is sometimes flushed first for much less; a leaking one cannot be. Vehicles with a rear heater have a second core that is quoted separately.
